{{Nihongo|'''Seiken-ji'''|清見寺|}},  is a {{ill|Buddhist temples in Japan|en|Buddhist temples in Japan|qid=Q3141900|lt=Buddhist temple}} belonging to the [[Myōshin-ji]] branch of the {{ill|Rinzai school|en|Rinzai school|qid=Q639625|lt=Rinzai school}} of {{ill|Japanese Zen|en|Japanese Zen|qid=Q189424|lt=Japanese Zen}}, located in the Okitsu neighborhood of {{ill|Shimizu-ku, Shizuoka|en|Shimizu-ku, Shizuoka|qid=Q79385|lt=Shimizu-ku}} ward of the city of {{ill|Shizuoka (city)|en|Shizuoka (city)|qid=Q174691|lt=Shizuoka (city)}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|qid=Q17|lt=Japan}}. Its [[honzon|main image]] is a statue of [[:en:Gautama Buddha|Shaka Nyōrai]]. It is also called Kiyomi-dera.

==History==
The temple claims to have been founded in the {{ill|Hakuchi (era)|en|Hakuchi (era)|qid=Q540118|lt=Hakuchi era}} of the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|qid=Q189178|lt=Nara period}} as a {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|qid=Q855964|lt=Tendai}} sect temple to protect the {{nihongo|Kiyomi-seki|清見関|}}, a natural barrier on the ancient {{ill|Tōkaidō (road)|en|Tōkaidō (road)|qid=Q963514|lt=Tōkaidō}} highway connecting the capital with eastern Japan, where the path of the road was a narrow ledge between cliffs and the {{ill|Pacific Ocean|en|Pacific Ocean|qid=Q98|lt=Pacific Ocean}}.  The temple subsequently fell into disrepair and was revived and converted to the Rinzai school by the monk {{ill|Enni|en|Enni|qid=Q739826|lt=Enni}} in 1262 AD. The temple flourished during the {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|qid=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}} and was named one of the [[Five Mountain System#The ''Jissetsu''|''Jissetsu'' temples]] in 1343. It is where {{ill|Ashikaga Takauji|en|Ashikaga Takauji|qid=Q297107|lt=Ashikaga Takauji}} and {{ill|Imagawa Yoshimoto|en|Imagawa Yoshimoto|qid=Q1054305|lt=Imagawa Yoshimoto}} took the tonsure. In the {{ill|Sengoku period|en|Sengoku period|qid=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period}}, when the young {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|qid=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu}} was held hostage in {{ill|Sunpu Domain|en|Sunpu Domain|qid=Q3034530|lt=Sunpu}} by the [[Imagawa clan]], he was sent to Seiken-ji to be tutored by the abbot {{ill|Sessai Chōrō|en|Sessai Chōrō|qid=Q842029|lt=Sessai Chōrō}}. During the invasion of {{ill|Suruga Province|en|Suruga Province|qid=Q864170|lt=Suruga Province}} by the [[Takeda clan]], {{ill|Imagawa Ujizane|en|Imagawa Ujizane|qid=Q3100078|lt=Imagawa Ujizane}} established his headquarters at this temple.

During the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|qid=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}, the temple continued to flourish due to its connection with Tokugawa Ieyasu, and its location on the Tōkaidō highway linking {{ill|Edo|en|Edo|qid=Q215646|lt=Edo}} with {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|qid=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}}. It was selected by the [[Tokugawa shogunate]] as one of the lodging spots for the {{ill|Joseon missions to Japan|en|Joseon missions to Japan|qid=Q15290174|lt=Joseon missions to Japan}} and the delegations from the {{ill|Ryukyu Kingdom|en|Ryukyu Kingdom|qid=Q28025|lt=Ryukyu Kingdom}}.  Due to these connections it was designated a [[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site of Japan]] in 1994.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/206953 |title=朝鮮通信使遺跡|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |accessdate=}}</ref> Surviving Edo period structures include the ''[[Sanmon]]'' (1651) and entrance to the {{ill|Main Hall (Japanese Buddhism)|en|Main Hall (Japanese Buddhism)|qid=Q17051413|lt=Main Hall}} (1616).<ref name="Shiseki">{{cite book |last1=Isomura |first1=Yukio |last2=Sakai |first2=Hideya |title=(国指定史跡事典) National Historic Site Encyclopedia |date=2012 |publisher=学生社 |isbn=978-4311750403}}{{in lang|ja}}</ref>

During the early {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}}, the tracks of the {{ill|Tōkaidō Main Line|en|Tōkaidō Main Line|qid=Q1190152|lt=Tōkaidō Main Line}} railway were laid across the front of the temple, which lost much of its properties. However, due to its scenic location overlooking {{ill|Suruga Bay|en|Suruga Bay|qid=Q1201023|lt=Suruga Bay}}, the temple drew the attention of poets and writers, including [[:en:Shimazaki Tōson|Shimazaki Tōson]], {{ill|Takayama Chogyū|en|Takayama Chogyū|qid=Q461853|lt=Takayama Chogyū}} and {{ill|Natsume Sōseki|en|Natsume Sōseki|qid=Q180903|lt=Natsume Sōseki}}.<ref name="Shiseki"/>

The temple was also the location of an important conference held by the leadership of the fledgling {{ill|Imperial Japanese Navy|en|Imperial Japanese Navy|qid=Q219712|lt=Imperial Japanese Navy}} in June 1887, with the participants discussing various tactics and {{ill|Naval strategy|en|Naval strategy|qid=Q11559269|lt=fleet maneuvers}}, which would then be tested in practice by the fleet in nearby Shimizu harbor.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Evans |first1=David C |last2=Peatty |first2=Mark |title=Kaigun: Strategy, Tactics, and Technology in the Imperial Japanese Navy, 1887-1941 |date=2012 |publisher=Naval Institute Press |isbn=978-1591142447 |pages=35–36}}</ref>

==Cultural properties==

===National Important Cultural Properties===
====Diary of Ye Mengde====
Diary of '''Ye Mengde''' ({{zh|t=葉夢得|w='''Yeh Meng-te'''}}; 1077–1148), a {{ill|Song dynasty|en|Song dynasty|qid=Q7462|lt=Song dynasty}} Chinese scholar, poet, and government minister, dated summer of 1149 AD<ref name="Bunka1">{{cite web |url= http://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/156808|title=宋版石林先生尚書伝 自巻第一至第四 紹興二十九年仲夏刊記|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |accessdate=}}</ref>

===National Place of Scenic Beauty===
==== Seiken-ji gardens====
The {{ill|Japanese garden|en|Japanese garden|qid=Q15835|lt=Japanese garden}} at Seiken-ji dates from the early Edo period and contains ponds and tree arrangements. It became a nationally designated [[Monuments of Japan|Place of Scenic Beauty]] in 1936.<ref name="Bunka2">{{cite web |url= http://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/162831|title=清見寺庭園|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |accessdate=}}</ref>
